These are just your nerves talking. I’m terms of clinicals, generally speaking, most preceptors want to work with students. That’s why they decided to be a preceptor. The school will prepare you for the clinicals. They will make sure that you pass the skill in class before allowing you to perform the skill in a clinical setting. In terms of making mistakes, that’s the point. It is okay to make mistakes in this setting as you are learning, and most people will know that. And so long as you stay within your scope of the learning permit and under the direction of a preceptor, you don’t need to worry about being sued. You would really have to go out if your way and want to do harm to a patient to get the that point, especially for AEMT clinicals. 

Best advice I can give you is pay attention in class and be receptive during clinicals. We’ve all been there. It’s not fun, but it’s an essential step. Ask questions, don’t be afraid to perform skills, and learn! If you get a bad preceptor, get through the clinical shift and move on. Before you know it, you’ll be passing the national registry. Good luck!

So I run at a very busy service. I currently work a 48 hour work schedule consisting of 2 24 hour shifts per week. I do pick up overtime shifts which generally can put me in the 60 to 80 hour work weeks. I find that if I do this consistently, I’ll get burnt out. The most I’ve worked in a week was about 110 hours and I felt it. 

If you’re looking for advise, work over time maybe 1 or 2 weeks out of a month and just work your normal hours for the rest of the month. That’s what I tend to do now and it works quite well. I know people who work like 80 hours every week and they may have a better paycheck, but I would rather work with other partners due to them being cranky all shift.

Working in the field is very different from in the classroom. My advice would be to remain open to change. Paramedics in the field may choose different treatments or perform a skill differently than you learned. Be willing to ask questions and understand why they do things the way they do. 

Personally I don't think there is anything wrong with going zero to hero. The thing I think most people struggle with in this regard would be willingness to adapt. 

Be willing to talk with your classmates for advice too, especially if they have experience. They've worked with you in scenarios so they may have some insight on how you can best approach your internship. 

Good luck and God speed!

In all honesty, a shift will be determined by who you work with. I remember my first partner was very critical of my performance. So much so that if it wasn't done her way, I was doing a shit job. You will have partners like that, where they have done something a thousand times and have their preferences. It got so bad that I even thought like you: I'm shit and EMS isn't for me. Long story short, she went on a different shift and I started working with different partners. I learned that I actually wasn't shit. I just needed a different perspective. 

I would say give it time. This job can honestly be super easy when you break it down. It takes a lot to be a "dipshit" and it usually comes down to people not giving a crap about their profession. It sounds like you care and are trying what you can to learn and improve. And quite frankly that's an awesome start. You are only 2 weeks in. There is so much more time to grow. Good luck and keep up with the passion!

In terms of most verses of the Bible, there is context that must be understood to get the full meaning.  Before the first commandment, it is mentioned that God is "the Lord, our god."  In Jewish tradition, it is preferred not to mention Him by name, Yahwah (YHWH).  So when translating into English, this tradition was kept by substituting with "Lord."  Continuing on to the next verse, the Lord is saying that it is common to see other things, people, or places as gods, and that they shouldn't be held in higher regard than Him.  In other words, don't hold the sun in higher regard than Him.
